Dear Waypoint Mobility Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Scientist, Demand Forecasting role on your Forecasting team. Since 2023, most of my work has been on transit ridership data. First I prepared it for planners, and later I forecast it. Waypoint builds forecasts that planners rely on every day, and that is the work I want to keep doing.

As a research assistant in Lakeshore University's Urban Analytics Lab, I built XGBoost and LightGBM models to forecast bus ridership. They used four years of automatic passenger counter data joined with anonymized mobility data. I led the feature engineering and model evaluation, and I'm first author of the resulting paper at the UrbanDS 2025 workshop. Compared with a SARIMA seasonal baseline, our model cut MAPE on a 2023 holdout from 14.2% to 9.8%. A reviewer raised possible leakage from the mobility features, so I re-ran the analysis with a two-week lag. Error rose to 10.4% but still clearly beat the baseline, and we reported both results. I used SHAP to explain what drove the forecasts: weekday, prior-week boardings, school calendar and mobility activity. I was also explicit about the limits, since we had data from one agency and only the post-pandemic period. I'd bring that same careful approach to evaluation to your stop-, route- and network-level models.

Before graduate school, I was a data analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the Tableau and SQL ridership dashboards used by the planning department. I also automated a weekly reporting pipeline in Python, which cut preparation from about six hours a week to one. That job taught me how planners read numbers and what makes them trust a forecast. Two semesters as a TA for a statistics course for non-majors sharpened my ability to explain technical results simply.

This summer at Northpoint Insurance, I built a gradient-boosted churn model that raised validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76 over a logistic regression baseline. I calibrated its probabilities with isotonic regression. Then I presented the results to the retention team and a VP in business terms: which customer segments to prioritize for outreach. The model was handed off to the retention analytics team for further evaluation. The experience I most want to gain next is taking a model all the way into production, and working with Waypoint's engineers to do that is a big part of why this role appeals to me.

I'll finish my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore in December 2026. I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I could contribute to Waypoint's forecasting work.

Sincerely,
Morgan Reyes

# Statement of Purpose: PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences

When I first worked with mobility data as a research assistant, I wanted to know how it was collected. The vendor's documentation said it came from SDKs in partner apps, with one-time opt-in consent. Our team was using those device pings, aggregated to block groups, to improve bus ridership forecasts. The work was legitimate and the forecasts got better. But I kept thinking about the people who tapped "allow" on a phone screen. I doubted any of them pictured their movements feeding a transit agency's planning model. That question has stayed with me since. Most of my training has been in building models, and I now want to study the people around them: those whose data goes in, and those who act on what comes out. That is why I am applying to the HCI PhD program at Khoury.

**Building models, and noticing what they leave out**

From January to December 2025, I worked part-time in Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab at Lakeshore University. I built gradient-boosted models (XGBoost and LightGBM) to forecast bus ridership, using four years of automatic passenger counter data joined with anonymized mobility data. I led feature engineering and evaluation and wrote the first draft of our paper. I am first author of the paper, which was accepted as a non-archival workshop paper at UrbanDS 2025. Our model cut MAPE on a 2023 holdout from 14.2% to 9.8% compared with a SARIMA baseline.

The parts of that project I learned most from were not about accuracy. A reviewer questioned whether the one-week-lagged mobility features leaked information. I re-ran the analysis with a two-week lag and reported the worse number (10.4%) next to the better one. When I prepared the talk, I organized it around the planners who would use the forecasts. I asked what they would need to trust the model, and what they should not trust it for. Our limitations section stated that the results covered one agency and only the post-pandemic period. Each time, the hard question was about people: who is represented in the data, who reads the output, and what they will assume.

Before graduate school, I was a data analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority from 2023 to 2024. I maintained the ridership dashboards used by the planning department. The technical side was simple. The real work was figuring out what a planner or a board member would take from a chart in the few seconds they looked at it. I didn't have words for it then, but that was an HCI problem.

**A first try at studying people**

In Spring 2026, I took Human-Centered Data Science as an elective. My team of three ran think-aloud usability sessions with five classmates using an AutoML dashboard, and I wrote the findings section of our report. It was a small class study, but the results surprised me. Participants accepted the top-ranked model without checking its metrics. Nobody opened the feature-importance panel. Two participants assumed the tool already "knew" which columns were sensitive. These were data science students, the kind of users the tool was designed for. They handed their judgment to the interface in exactly the places where judgment mattered most.

That project showed me two things. First, the questions I care about can be studied rigorously, with methods I only began learning that semester. Second, I need much more training in those methods. Five participants and a course report are a start, not a research program.

**What I want to study**

I am still forming my research direction, and I expect the first years of a PhD to shape it. Broadly, I am interested in how people understand, rely on, and consent to data-driven systems. Two threads come from my experience so far:

- **Consent and comprehension for secondary data use.** I want to know what people believe they are agreeing to when their app data is reused for things like transit planning. I also want to understand how consent interfaces and data documentation could close the gap between that belief and what actually happens.
- **Calibrated reliance on ML tools.** I want to understand why practitioners and decision-makers over-trust ranked outputs and defaults, as my AutoML participants did. I want to explore which interface and explanation designs help them question a model at the right moments.

My quantitative background would help here. I can build the systems I would study, and I am comfortable with the statistics that mixed-methods work needs. My training in qualitative methods and study design is limited. That is the gap I most want a PhD to close.

**Why Khoury**

[Placeholder: name 1–3 Khoury HCI faculty whose recent work connects to these threads, with one specific sentence per person on how it relates. I can look up current faculty and recent papers if you want. Please verify any names before submitting.] Khoury's interdisciplinary approach to HCI and its connections to Boston's public sector would let me keep my work tied to real deployments, like the transit systems I started with.

Teaching STAT 1100, a statistics course for non-majors, for two semesters also showed me that I enjoy helping people reason about data they didn't produce. I would like a career, whether in academia or applied research, where that sits at the center of the work.

I am finishing my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University in December 2026 and am applying for Fall 2027 entry.

---

A few things for you to decide before you send this:

1. **The opening uses your comment about mobility-data consent** from the RA project. It's the most honest reason you've given me for wanting HCI. But Prof. Patel is writing you a letter, so check that the framing isn't critical of the lab's work. I left out the "home-area" feature you tried and dropped, because it could read as re-identifying riders.
2. **I kept the claims accurate.** The usability study is a class project with five participants. The paper is a non-archival workshop paper. I didn't mention the rail follow-up, since you weren't keen on it.
3. **The research directions are kept loose** because you said you're still unsure. Change them if either thread doesn't feel like yours.
4. **The "Why Khoury" part needs real faculty names.** Check Khoury's length limit too, since this is around 900 words.

# Statement of Purpose: PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences

In my first semester as a research assistant, I was building features from anonymized mobility data: phone location pings, aggregated to neighborhoods, used to forecast bus ridership. At some point I looked up how the vendor collected the data. It came from apps that asked users once for permission to share their location. I remember thinking: *I doubt anyone tapping "allow" pictured this.*

I kept working on the project, and it was good work. But that thought stayed with me more than anything about the model. I've realized it's a question I want to spend years on. Not how to make the forecast better, but what people understand about the systems that use their data, and what the people using those systems understand about them.

I came to this through numbers. I studied economics, then worked for a year as a data analyst at a regional transit agency, then started a master's in data science. My favorite part of the analyst job was trying to make a ridership dashboard make sense to the agency's board. The SQL behind it was easy. The hard part was guessing what someone would conclude from a chart they'd look at for ten seconds, and whether that conclusion would be right. I didn't know then that this was a research question. I thought it was just part of the job.

When my research project ended, my advisor offered me a follow-up forecasting project. I realized I didn't want it. I liked the people in the lab and I liked the work, but what I actually cared about was everything around the model: whose data went in, who would read the output, and what they would assume.

So I took a Human-Centered Data Science course, and for the first time I studied people directly. My team ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML tool. It was a small class project, but what we saw surprised me. People accepted whichever model the tool ranked first. Nobody opened the panel explaining what the model relied on. Two people assumed the tool already knew which data was sensitive. These were data science students, the people the tool was designed for. They trusted it in exactly the places they shouldn't have. Writing up those findings was the most engaged I've felt in my master's program.

Teaching pointed the same way. For two semesters I was a TA for a statistics course for non-majors. The part of grading I cared about most was the interpretation: whether a student could say what their numbers meant for an actual decision. That's the gap I keep running into, between what data says and what people take from it.

I don't have a finished research agenda, and I'd rather say so than invent one. The questions I keep coming back to are:

- What do people think they agreed to when their data gets reused for something they never imagined?
- Why do people, experts included, defer to an algorithm's top answer?
- What would it take for an interface to help them push back at the right moments?

These questions are about people and AI, not just about building models.

My background is mostly technical, and I know that is both an asset and a gap. I can build the kinds of systems I'd want to study, and I'm comfortable with the statistics. What I don't have yet is serious training in qualitative methods and study design. That's a big part of why I want a PhD rather than another job.

[Why Khoury: 1–2 faculty whose work connects to consent or reliance on AI, one sentence each in your own words about why their work interests you.]

I finish my M.S. in December 2026 and am applying for Fall 2027 entry.

---

I can only partly fix the "sound like me" problem, because most of what I know about you comes from project work. Answering any of these, even roughly, would help me most:

1. **When did you first think "maybe research about people, not models"?** Was the mobility data moment really the start, or was it something earlier, like economics, the transit job, or a person?
2. **Did anything in the AutoML sessions or in office hours stick with you?** A specific person or moment would bring the statement to life more than any summary.
3. **How do you sound when you explain this to a friend?** Wry, earnest or blunt? The quotes I used ("I doubt anyone tapping 'allow' pictured this," "people and AI, not just building models") are the only samples of your voice I have.

Two things to check before you use this draft:
- **The follow-up project paragraph** says honestly that you didn't want another forecasting project. Prof. Patel is writing you a letter, so read it with that in mind. I kept the tone warm toward the lab.
- **The draft says the AutoML write-up was the most engaged you felt in your master's program, and that interpretation was what you cared about most when grading.** I took those from what you've told me, but I don't have your exact words for them. Cut or change them if they're not true.

# Statement of Purpose: PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences

In 2025 I was a research assistant on a bus ridership forecasting project. At one point I tried a feature that combined two columns. One was the stop where a frequent rider usually first boarded. The other was the area where their phone tended to be at night. Both came from data described as anonymized. Together, they put a lot of riders on just a few blocks.

The feature didn't improve the model, so I dropped it. Nobody did anything wrong. But afterward I looked up how the phone data had been collected. It came from partner apps, through a one-time "allow." I doubt anyone tapping that pictured a transit model, or two columns that together could narrow them down to a block.

That is where my interest in HCI started. Since then I keep coming back to one question: what do people think can be figured out from what they share, and could they ever actually see it? That used to mean apps. Now it also means AI tools that people talk to, about a lot more than where they sleep.

My background is mostly in numbers. I studied economics, then worked for a year as a data analyst at a regional transit agency. I am now finishing a master's in data science. I'm comfortable building models. That feature was when I noticed that the part I cared about wasn't the model.

The closest I have come to studying this directly was a class project in Human-Centered Data Science. My team of three ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML tool. Several things came up, but one stuck. Two participants assumed the tool already knew which columns were sensitive. It didn't.

It felt like the same problem from the other side. People who share data assume not much can be inferred from it. People who build with data assume the system will catch what's sensitive. Neither can see what the system can actually work out, so they fill the gap with an assumption.

It was five people in a class project, and I don't want to make more of it than it is. But it was the first time I had a method for asking the question instead of just having it.

I don't have a clear research question yet. I have a cluster of them, and I expect the first years of a PhD to narrow them down:

- What do people believe can be inferred from the data they share, and how far off are they?
- Can an interface show someone what could be learned from their data, in a way they understand, before they agree to share it?
- How does this change with conversational AI, where people share more, more casually, and the inferences are harder to see?
- On the builder side, what do practitioners assume their tools handle for them, and what happens when they're wrong?

What I bring is time on the side that builds these things. I know how easy it is to combine two harmless-looking columns, and how little anyone downstream would notice. What I lack is training in qualitative methods, study design, and the privacy and HCI literature. That is the main reason I want a PhD rather than another job.

[Why Khoury: 1–2 faculty whose work touches privacy, inference, or how people understand AI systems. Write one plain sentence each on what in their work connects to the questions above.]

I finish my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University in December 2026 and am applying for Fall 2027 entry.

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah † , Tianshi Li †

NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track)

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while a constellation of more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. This position paper argues that the privacy landscape of LLM systems extends far beyond training data extraction, encompassing risks from data collection practices, inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent capabilities, and the democratization of surveillance through deep inference attacks. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of privacy risks across the LLM lifecycle -- from data collection through deployment -- and demonstrate through case studies how current privacy frameworks fail to address these multifaceted threats. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,322 AI/ML privacy papers published at leading conferences over the past decade (2016--2025), we reveal that while memorization receives outsized attention in technical research, the most pressing privacy harms lie elsewhere, where current technical approaches offer little traction and viable paths forward remain unclear. We call for a fundamental shift in how the research community approaches LLM privacy, moving beyond the narrow focus of current technical solutions and embracing interdisciplinary approaches that address the sociotechnical nature of these emerging threats.

Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment

Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Raio Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li

Preprint

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. Each task is specified by an authorization contract that separates the principal's instruction, completion criteria, and out-of-authorization actions. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged (19.3% at low effort versus 19.1% at high effort), with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p = 0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment, motivating it as a distinct target for agent evaluation and development. AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

arXiv

-->

Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li

COLM 2026

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users' behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. Yet the expanded design space of agent autonomy also presents opportunities to shape these effects, which remain underexplored. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization's effects on users' privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control back to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, improves users' perceived control. This in turn attenuates personalization's adverse effects: privacy concerns rise less and trust declines less. Our results suggest that designing agent's autonomy that supports human autonomy (both perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns. This positions aligning decision authority between users and agents (autonomy alignment) as an important opportunity and challenge for trustworthy human-agent interaction.

Tianshi Li is an assistant professor in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences at Northeastern University, based in Boston.

After obtaining her doctorate in human–computer interaction, Li joined UC Berkeley as a postdoctoral scholar, where she continued her research on usable privacy and security in mobile apps and explored novel privacy issues in human–LLM interactions. Li also worked at Google, where she applied her techniques to products that provide privacy compliance support to companies. Specifically, she developed a series of integrated development environment plugins to assist developers in building mobile apps with native privacy support by adding privacy annotations to their source code. Li is particularly interested in enabling developers who don’t specialize in privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness to create apps that still meet privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness requirements. She has published work at the CHI, IMWUT/UbiComp, CSCW, and PETS conferences, as well as the TOCHI journal, and has earned several “best paper” honors.

Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human privacy preferences requires capturing individuals’ disclosure boundaries beyond general privacy norms. However, current models lack methods for eliciting such nuanced preferences and ground truth data to evaluate alignment in realistic settings. We introduce CIDER, a dataset of 14,850 human annotations from 169 users, forming 1,650 contextual disclosure boundary sets across 60 interpersonal communication scenarios where information sharing violates privacy norms. Each boundary represents a real user’s disclosure decisions over 9 sharing variants, given a communication role and AI-mediated condition. We formulate a prediction task in which models predict a user’s disclosure decision from historical boundaries, with varying levels of contextual information. Across eight open and proprietary models, personalization improves performance, with accuracy gains of up to 11.41% using six in-context examples. However, these gains arise from different mechanisms. Larger models such as GPT-5.4 (with medium reasoning effort) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 leverage semantic context to infer user-specific, context-dependent disclosure preferences for more accurate predictions, while smaller models tend to rely on structured heuristics based on disclosure granularity and identifiability and present trade-offs between false positives and false negatives. Our findings highlight the potential and limitations of current LLMs’ privacy modeling capability and position CIDER as a resource for advancing personalized privacy preference alignment.

Dear Prof. Li,

I'm finishing an M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University and applying to the Khoury HCI PhD program for Fall 2027. I'm writing because your lab's work is close to the question I want to study, and I'd like to know if you're taking students this cycle.

My interest started on a bus ridership forecasting project. I tried a feature that combined a frequent rider's usual first boarding stop with where their phone tended to be at night. Both columns came from data described as anonymized. Together, they put a lot of riders on just a few blocks. The feature didn't help the model, so I dropped it. But the consent behind the phone data was a one-time "allow" in a partner app. Since then I keep wondering what people think can be figured out from what they share, with apps and now with AI tools they talk to. I also wonder whether they could ever actually see it.

That's why AgentDoxx and your position paper on LLM privacy across the lifecycle stood out to me. Both treat inference and re-identification as more pressing than memorization. CIDER covers the other half of what I care about: people's own boundaries for what they disclose, compared with what can actually be inferred about them.

My background is mostly quantitative. I have a BA in economics and worked for a year as a data analyst at a transit agency. I'm first author of a workshop paper on ridership forecasting at UrbanDS 2025. In a human-centered data science course, I worked on a small think-aloud study of an AutoML tool. Two of the participants assumed the tool already knew which columns were sensitive. I don't have a settled research question yet, and my training in qualitative methods is thin. That's a big part of why I want a PhD.

My portfolio is at github.com/example-morgan. If you're recruiting, I'd appreciate a short conversation, or any sense of whether my interests fit the lab.

Thank you for your time.

Best,
Morgan Reyes
M.S. Data Science, Lakeshore University
